hero.headline: Florida Supreme Court adopts new AI courtroom rules after rampant misuse
hero.body:
Florida's highest court has adopted new rules requiring attorneys and self-represented litigants to certify that any evidence or case law they present in court actually exists and is accurate. The rules take effect June 15 in response to what legal and artificial intelligence experts describe as a growing crisis of AI misuse in courtrooms. Violators could face sanctions ranging from public reprimand to fines and suspension.

The problem has become serious enough that Florida's Supreme Court felt compelled to act. Federal Judge William Matthewman, chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, has worked to address AI misuse in his own courtroom and remains concerned about the trajectory. "Unfortunately, I see it getting worse before it gets better. I think the Florida Supreme Court's order will help in Florida, but I unfortunately have seen over the last couple of years that it is growing and growing and growing," Matthewman said. He cautioned that lawyers and self-represented parties should verify everything they file. "I would caution lawyers and parties representing themselves to make sure everything you file in court is accurate, because if not, you could find yourself in hot water," he said.

A recent case in Polk County illustrates the problem. An attorney representing the Polk County School District filed a motion to dismiss in a school bus camera lawsuit containing fabricated facts and citations to cases that do not exist. The attorney apologized and stated he used ChatGPT as a drafting and research aid but had no excuse for failing to verify the information before filing. The school district said it takes accuracy and integrity seriously and is reviewing whether the attorney will continue receiving contracted work. Paul Figueroa, a Tampa criminal defense attorney who recently began using AI to improve his workflow, acknowledged the technology's limitations. "It can be something as simple as it gives a quote that's directly on point to my case, and you go, all right, this is brilliant, this is what I've been looking for, I could have searched 300 cases and not come up with anything better than this, and then you realize that's not in the case," Figueroa said. When asked if the new rules go far enough, he replied, "I do. I think it goes far enough for what we know now."

The consequences of AI misuse have extended beyond courtroom documents. Earlier this year, a Florida woman was jailed after a fake AI-generated text was used against her, though she was later cleared of all charges. In another case, a St. Petersburg woman created an AI-generated photo of a man she falsely claimed had burglarized and raped her. She later admitted the claim was fabricated, telling police, "I lied about it."

cards.headline: Fertilizer Ban Begins June 1 in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River Counties
cards.body:
Starting June 1, residents and businesses in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties must stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. The seasonal restriction continues through the rainy season and applies to both residential and commercial applications. Anyone maintaining a lawn, garden, or landscaped area in these three counties will need to put fertilizer use on hold until the ban is lifted.

The ban targets a significant environmental concern in the region. Jordan Skaggs, who works with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that nutrient-rich runoff during heavy rains can trigger algae blooms in local waterways including the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. These blooms create serious problems for aquatic ecosystems. They can block sunlight from reaching plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. In some cases, when algae blooms reach high concentrations, they produce toxins that threaten not only wildlife but also human health and the overall health of the ecosystem.

The counties implemented this ban as a preventive measure during the season when rainfall is heaviest. The nitrogen and phosphorus in fertilizers act as nutrients that fuel algae growth in waterways. By restricting these products during months when runoff is most likely to occur, the counties hope to reduce the amount of these nutrients reaching local rivers and lagoons. This approach targets the source of the problem rather than trying to manage blooms after they develop.

For people who want to maintain their landscapes during the ban, alternatives exist. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical solution. According to Ricketts, composting provides nutrients to gardens and landscaping in a way that works within the seasonal restrictions. He noted that even something as simple as a small trash can can serve as an effective composting system. This method offers an accessible way for homeowners and landscapers to keep their plants healthy while supporting the environmental goals of the fertilizer ban. Those looking to learn more about composting techniques and other alternatives can reach out to local extension offices for guidance on maintaining their landscapes responsibly during the restricted season.

cards.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks for 250th anniversary due to severe drought
cards.body:
Florida's upcoming Fourth of July celebrations for the nation's 250th anniversary could be dramatically altered by severe drought conditions gripping the state. State officials are carefully monitoring the situation to determine whether a statewide fireworks ban will be necessary. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services has indicated that current drought severity exceeds conditions from 1998, the last time the state implemented such a ban.

Every county in Florida is experiencing at least abnormally dry conditions. Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast face particularly challenging circumstances, with areas there dealing with moderate to extreme drought conditions. In May, Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson provided an early warning about the possibility of restricting fireworks. Simpson emphasized the scale of the potential risk, stating "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time." He acknowledged the historic importance of the 250th anniversary celebration but encouraged residents to consider other ways to mark the occasion.

Despite the concerning outlook, some businesses remain cautiously optimistic about the situation. Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach has already experienced higher customer traffic as people shop early for the holiday. Bill Murphy from the store explained that the business closely tracks drought conditions to ensure adequate ground moisture levels. Murphy noted that weather forecasts suggest significant rainfall ahead, which could help alleviate the current crisis. The store continues to monitor the drought index carefully while maintaining hope that conditions will improve.

The Department of Agriculture has made clear that implementing a fireworks ban would represent a last resort option if conditions do not improve. State leaders are actively watching drought developments as the Fourth of July approaches to make their final decision about restrictions. The decision will ultimately depend on whether conditions improve before the holiday arrives. Florida's communities, both coastal and inland, remain united in dealing with the statewide drought that affects every region.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion so severe ocean could breach island at Peck Lake, state warns
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report has documented critical erosion across nearly the entire 11.5-mile coastline of Jupiter Island, raising concerns that a future ocean breakthrough at Peck Lake could split the barrier island in half. The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development already faces risk, to Peck Lake, where a breach would transform a narrow strip of land into an open inlet. This scenario has happened before: a storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s until the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers refilled the area with sand.

According to Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society, a future breach would disrupt ecosystems dependent on a precise balance between fresh and saltwater. The state report identifies numerous sites at risk, including the Joseph Reed Mound, an archaeological site between 3,000 and 4,000 years old that has already lost half its area to erosion. Three wildlife refuges face similar threats: Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry noted that more than 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. A second state assessment warns that erosion is also destroying mangrove swamps essential for habitat and coastal protection, while rising water levels could displace entire species on the island.

The Town of Jupiter Island combats erosion through continuous maintenance efforts. In April 2025, officials completed a major beach renourishment project that deposited enough sand to equal nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said no oceanfront homes face immediate danger only because of ongoing work. He described the situation candidly: "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over. We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it." The town currently spends about $3 million annually in taxpayer dollars on beach renourishment.

The sustainability of this approach remains uncertain. Field warned that a potential breach would require massive state and federal investment to repair. "We would have cataclysmic erosion if we didn't get federal funding and state funding," he said. He emphasized that if beach renourishment funding disappears across Florida, the state's entire coastline could transform rapidly and unfavorably. Field believes the recent FDEP assessment strengthens Jupiter Island's position to secure state and federal funding to address the erosion crisis. The report ultimately underscores how coastal erosion threatens not just homes and infrastructure, but also irreplaceable natural and historical resources.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowner watches burglary live on security camera, suspect arrested
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie resident watched a masked man burglarize his apartment in real time on his home security camera Thursday afternoon. Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was arrested and charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling following the incident at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail. The incident began around 3:38 p.m. when the apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home. After checking his live camera feed and spotting the masked intruder, the resident activated his camera's audible siren, causing the suspect to leave briefly. Thibodeau returned and tampered with the camera itself.

Multiple witnesses saw the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. Port St. Lucie Police arrived to find clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Thibodeau exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from multiple sources throughout the complex, including doorbell cameras that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. Police found evidence that Thibodeau had attempted to obstruct security cameras and that a watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen during the burglary.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban starts June 1 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
cards.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. The restriction remains in effect through September 30, covering the region's rainy season when nutrient runoff poses the greatest environmental risk.

The ban targets a significant environmental problem. According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the goal is to reduce nutrient-rich runoff that flows into local waterways during heavy rains. This runoff can trigger harmful algae blooms in sensitive ecosystems like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. Skaggs explained that these blooms create multiple problems for aquatic environments. "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," Skaggs said. The impacts can be severe depending on bloom density. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health."

Residents should prepare alternatives now to maintain their landscaping during the ban period. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical solution. This method provides essential nutrients to gardens and landscaping without violating the restriction on commercial fertilizers. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." Composting allows homeowners to recycle organic materials while supporting healthy plant growth.

The four-month ban reflects growing awareness of how fertilizer runoff damages Florida's waterways. By restricting nutrient applications during the season when heavy rainfall washes chemicals into rivers and lagoons, the three counties aim to protect both environmental and public health. Residents who plan ahead by starting compost systems or exploring other organic alternatives can maintain their landscaping without contributing to the algae bloom problem.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island Erosion Could Split Island in Half at Peck Lake, State Report Warns
cards.teaser: A new state report found the entire 11.5-mile shoreline of Jupiter Island has eroded so severely the ocean could breach at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that nearly the entire 11.5-mile coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, threatening roads, buildings, drainage systems, natural habitats, wildlife, and ancient sites. The erosion stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could split the island in half by turning a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater. "We're going to probably have more storm surges that would create more of these breaks," Perry said. Among the sites at risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry noted there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in those areas.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues fighting erosion through constant maintenance and beach renourishment. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project. About $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment annually. "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," Field said. "We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it." Field warned that without federal and state funding, the island could experience "cataclysmic erosion."

cards.headline: Okeechobee County Woman Sues Campbell Soup and Walmart Over Alleged Worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard claims she and her daughter found live worms in SpaghettiOs after eating them and developed parasitic infections. The alleged incident occurred in June 2024 when she bought the product at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart after she and her daughter allegedly found live worms in SpaghettiOs purchased in June 2024 at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the complaint, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. Attorneys for Hubbard said she documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product.

Hubbard claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications following the incident. The lawsuit alleges Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart failed to properly inspect the product. The case seeks $50,000 in damages and was filed in Okeechobee County. Campbell said the claims lack merit, while Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Florida Voters Weigh Property Tax Proposal Ahead of November Ballot
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide in November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes on homeowners, a proposal drawing mixed reactions in West Palm Beach. The ballot measure requires 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018. How much money cities and counties would lose under the plan remains under calculation, and it is unknown where budget cuts would fall if the measure passes.

Brian Edington supports the proposal because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida. "I think it's a really good idea because it saves the people that really live in Florida, the homeowners," Edington said. He is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his neighborhood as an example of where cuts could be made. "I have trash services in my neighborhood, they pick it up twice, I don't need it twice a week, once a week would be adequate," Edington said. Rosabella Olivares expressed concern about reduced funding, saying "There's going to be less money ... because everything is expensive now." While homeowners were generally supportive of paying less in taxes, renters expressed skepticism. A resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said savings would not reach renters, stating the landlords would raise rent on everybody.

cards.headline: Florida dive operators fight federal shark feeding ban they say could devastate conservation tourism
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry, with operators warning it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses.
cards.body:
The Safe Florida Seas Act, H.R. 3831, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters call it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, a coalition of dive operators argues the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education, conservation and responsible shark encounters, while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said operators are requesting the chance to present data and explain their practices. He emphasized they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats for food compared to commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface.

The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent. However, Florida operators and some researchers point to different outcomes in Hawaii since the ban. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased, fatalities have been reported and, according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch.

cards.headline: Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties could lose $283 million under property tax referendum
cards.teaser: A new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption could cost the three Treasure Coast counties a combined $283 million in the first year alone, according to estimates from the Florida Association of Counties.
cards.body:
A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimates that Treasure Coast counties could face significant revenue losses if voters approve the property tax reform referendum in November. Martin County would lose $50 million in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29, St. Lucie County would lose $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29, and Indian River County would lose $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said local officials are working with administrators and the Office of Management and Budget to determine the full impact. "If there's a cut when it comes to property taxes, there's going to be some real shortfalls, some real challenges and some revenue is going to have to be made up somewhere," Powell said. Options to offset losses could include increased sales taxes, higher user fees for services, or budget cuts. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal would provide relief for struggling families in $300,000 homes working multiple jobs to make ends meet.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway to make way for 300,000-square-foot mixed-use development
cards.teaser: Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week as the first phase of a revitalization project for the shopping center gets underway.
cards.body:
Crews began demolishing portions of the Indian River Mall this week as the first phase of a revitalization project gets underway. Project manager Joseph Scarfone said workers are currently taking down the Macy's building and will soon demolish the former Sears location. The site will be transformed into a new indoor and outdoor shopping center with approximately 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. Scarfone described the future development as "a city within a city," replacing what he characterized as a dead mall that had been collecting cobwebs for the last 12 years.

Neighbors watching the demolition from the parking lot expressed support for the project. Mary Alice Stopyra, a neighbor, said she was happy to see the degraded building torn down. Mark Manera, a Vero Beach resident who has visited the mall for years, described witnessing a steady decline year after year. He said the change could bring new life, new jobs and new opportunity to the area. Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, though the project team is still working on permitting for the remaining phases of the development.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island could split in half as erosion threatens to breach Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A new state report warns that nearly the entire coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean threatening to break through at Peck Lake and potentially split the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could breach at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The erosion threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater.

The report identifies multiple sites at risk, including the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, as well as Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry noted over 33 threatened and endangered species are at risk in those areas. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town spends about $3 million in taxpayer dollars annually on beach renourishment and completed a major project in April 2025. Field stated that without continued state and federal funding, "the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly."

cards.headline: Okeechobee County woman sues Campbell Soup, Walmart over alleged worms in SpaghettiOs
cards.teaser: Mary Hubbard of Okeechobee County is suing Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart, claiming she and her daughter found live worms in their SpaghettiOs after eating them and developed parasitic infections.
cards.body:
Mary Hubbard from Okeechobee County claims she and her daughter developed parasitic infections and other medical complications after eating SpaghettiOs purchased in June 2024 at the Walmart Supercenter on South Parrott Avenue in Okeechobee. According to the lawsuit, Hubbard discovered what appeared to be worms or parasites actively moving within the food. She documented the contamination in multiple videos that clearly depict worm-like organisms moving within the food product, according to the complaint.

The lawsuit, which seeks $50,000 in damages, alleges that Campbell Soup Co. and Walmart failed to properly inspect the product. Campbell said the claims lack merit, and Walmart said it is reviewing the court filing.

cards.headline: Florida considering statewide fireworks ban for Fourth of July over drought concerns
cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services says this year's drought is more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was put in place, raising concerns for Fourth of July celebrations.
cards.body:
Florida's Fourth of July celebrations could look dramatically different this year as state leaders weigh a potential statewide fireworks ban due to severe drought conditions. The entire state of Florida is at least abnormally dry, with Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services notes this year's drought is even more severe than 1998, the last time a statewide fireworks ban was implemented.

Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning in May about the possibility of a ban. "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in an evening all over the state all at one time," Simpson said. While acknowledging the significance of the state's 250th celebration of American independence, Simpson urged residents to consider alternatives. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, representative Bill Murphy reported increased customer activity as people shop early. Murphy said the store monitors the drought index closely but remains cautiously optimistic, citing plenty of rain in the forecast. The Department of Agriculture said a fireworks ban would be a last resort.

cards.headline: Florida shark dive operators fight federal ban on shark feeding in state waters
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast within 200 miles is drawing sharp criticism from shark diving operators, including those based in Florida, who warn it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses.
cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body

H.R. 3831, known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. A coalition of dive operators, including veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education and conservation, says the bill unfairly targets their work while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said no one from Congress has asked operators to present data or explain their practices. Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food compared to some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface. The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent, but Florida operators and some researchers say the experience tells a different story. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased and fatalities have been reported.

hero.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach for new mixed-use development
hero.teaser: Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project for the shopping center.
hero.body:
Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week to make way for a revitalization project for the shopping center. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager working on the redevelopment project, said crews are working on the first phase, taking down the Macys and soon the area where the Sears used to be.

Vero Beach neighbor Mary Alice Stopyra said she is happy the mall is being torn down. Mark Manera from Vero Beach said he has been coming to the mall for years and has watched it decline year after year.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. Manera said the change brings new life, new jobs and new opportunity.

Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be done by 2027. The project team is still working on permitting for the rest of the project.

cards.headline: Martin County faces $50 million property tax loss under state referendum
cards.teaser: Government officials are working to assess the impact of the new property tax reform referendum that would raise the homestead exemption and lower property tax bills.
cards.body:
A recent study from the Florida Association of Counties estimated potential property tax losses across the region if a homestead exemption referendum passes. Martin County faces $50 million in losses in 2027-28 and $93 million in 2028-29. St. Lucie County faces $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County faces $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. Okeechobee County faces $4 million in 2027-28 and $7 million in 2028-29.

Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said if property taxes are cut, there will be real shortfalls and real challenges, and some revenue will have to be made up somewhere. Powell said options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are possibilities, though he noted officials do not yet know if solutions will include an increase in sales tax, user fees, or other services. The referendum to raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 will be decided by voters in November. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, said the proposal is a break for struggling families in homes assessed at $300,000 working multiple jobs.

cards.headline: Florida voters split on property tax proposal ahead of November vote
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide in November whether to raise the homestead exemption to roll back property taxes, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure requires 60% approval to pass, following a similar failed proposal in 2018. The exact amount cities and counties would lose remains under calculation, with budget cut locations still unknown.

Brian Edington supports the proposal because it benefits permanent Florida homeowners. He said he is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his own neighborhood as an example, suggesting trash pickup could be reduced from twice weekly to once weekly. Rosabella Olivares, a shopper in West Palm Beach, expressed concern about reduced funding, saying "there's going to be less money because everything is expensive now." A resident named Stan opposed complete funding elimination, citing the importance of infrastructure. Homeowners generally supported lower taxes, but renters expressed skepticism. One renter along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach predicted landlords would raise rents on all renters if the measure passes.

cards.headline: Glades Day Gators chase first state football title since 2010
cards.teaser: The Glades Day Gators are sweating through summer training in Belle Glade with one goal in mind: a return to state championship glory.
cards.body:
The Glades Day Gators are putting in the work this summer, sweating through the heat and humidity in Belle Glade with one goal in mind: a return to state championship glory. The Gators finished last season with a 4-9 record, but made a run in the SSAA playoffs, reaching the third round before their season ended. Head coach James Threlkeld said the playoff push offered a valuable lesson. "The way we were able to turn it around in the playoffs, you know, that was a lesson learned," Threlkeld said. "I think, more for our kids, that was just kind of a decision they made, so we're trying to carry over that mindset."

Threlkeld said the summer months are a critical part of building toward a strong fall campaign. "Getting yourself acclimated to the heat and the humidity is only gonna help us whenever we start camping," Threlkeld said. "You know they have helmets and pads on, you know I think that's a key part." The Gators last won a state title in 2010. Senior Ramsey Rimes said adding another championship would be meaningful for his final year. "It would be a great senior year if we finish it off," Rimes said. "Hopefully, we got it this year." Fellow senior Preston Sanford said breaking the streak would mean a lot to the program.

hero.headline: 80-Mile Ocean Paddle From Bimini to Lake Worth Beach Set for June 13 to Raise Cystic Fibrosis Funds
hero.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of open Atlantic Ocean from Bimini, Bahamas to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis fundraiser.
hero.body:
Participants will launch from Bimini at midnight on June 13 and arrive at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. The endurance trek benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, which event founder Travis Suit established in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On June 11, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and a community buffet dinner. June 12 brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before launch night.

All paddlers must wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, with crew or virtual participants having a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong beach celebration marking the paddlers' arrival.

cards.headline: Beetlejuice the Musical Performs Final Shows at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach Through Saturday
cards.body:
"Beetlejuice" the musical brings Tim Burton's 1988 film to the stage at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach through June 7. Actor Ryan Stajmiger plays the mischievous demon Beetlejuice, a character who appears for only 15 minutes in the original film. "I've loved the movie since I was a kid. I'm a huge Tim Burton fan, and you know, Michael Keaton's performance is so iconic," Stajmiger said. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble. The production features spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments.

One of Stajmiger's favorite aspects of performing is interacting directly with the audience. "I get to break the fourth wall a lot, so I get to communicate directly to the audience and share some moments with them. That's my favorite part of theater," he explained. Early in the run, Stajmiger experienced an unexpected onstage moment when his wig change went wrong. "I have a wig change on stage that I'm wearing two wigs. The second wig came off with the first wig, so I was bald for an entire scene." Rather than letting the mishap derail the performance, he adapted. Final performances include shows at 7:30 p.m. on June 3 and 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up with parental discretion advised.

hero.headline: Florida could ban Fourth of July fireworks for 250th anniversary due to severe drought
hero.body:
Florida's upcoming Fourth of July celebrations for the nation's 250th anniversary could be dramatically altered by severe drought conditions gripping the state. State officials are carefully monitoring the situation to determine whether a statewide fireworks ban will be necessary. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services has indicated that current drought severity exceeds conditions from 1998, the last time the state implemented such a ban.

Every county in Florida is experiencing at least abnormally dry conditions. Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast face particularly challenging circumstances, with areas there dealing with moderate to extreme drought conditions. In May, Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson provided an early warning about the possibility of restricting fireworks. Simpson emphasized the scale of the potential risk, stating "If we're still in drought conditions come Fourth of July, absolutely. We're talking about obviously, potentially hundreds of thousands of people going out doing fireworks. You could put the entire state on fire in evening all over the state all at one time." He acknowledged the historic importance of the 250th anniversary celebration but encouraged residents to consider other ways to mark the occasion.

Despite the concerning outlook, some businesses remain cautiously optimistic about the situation. Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach has already experienced higher customer traffic as people shop early for the holiday. Bill Murphy from the store explained that the business closely tracks drought conditions to ensure adequate ground moisture levels. Murphy noted that weather forecasts suggest significant rainfall ahead, which could help alleviate the current crisis. The store continues to monitor the drought index carefully while maintaining hope that conditions will improve.

The Department of Agriculture has made clear that implementing a fireworks ban would represent a last resort option if conditions do not improve. State leaders are actively watching drought developments as the Fourth of July approaches to make their final decision about restrictions. The decision will ultimately depend on whether conditions improve before the holiday arrives. Florida's communities, both coastal and inland, remain united in dealing with the statewide drought that affects every region.

cards.headline: Florida dive operators challenge federal shark feeding ban as House passes Safe Florida Seas Act
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida has cleared the U.S. House, drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry.
cards.body:
The Safe Florida Seas Act, H.R. 3831, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters have called it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, a coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work, which often includes veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education, conservation and responsible encounters with sharks, while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said no one from Congress has yet asked operators to present data or explain their practices. Operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives. They argue this is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food than some commercial harvesting operations that can release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface.

The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent. However, Florida operators and some researchers say the Hawaii experience tells a different story. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents have increased and fatalities have been reported. According to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. In a letter sent to Congress, Campbell urged senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Secretary of State Marco Rubio testifies to Florida congressional delegation on Cuba, Venezuela transitions
cards.teaser: Secretary of State Marco Rubio returned to Capitol Hill for meetings with Florida's congressional delegation, addressing timelines for government transitions in Cuba and Venezuela.
cards.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio returned to Capitol Hill to meet with Florida's congressional delegation, fielding questions from former Senate colleagues about U.S. policy in the Western Hemisphere. Sen. Rick Scott, a Naples Republican, praised the recent indictment of former Cuban President Raúl Castro and the arrest of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, saying Castro's indictment sparked renewed hope for a free Cuba with government accountability and political freedom. When Scott asked about the timeline for transitioning away from Maduro's government, Rubio noted that Vice President Delcy Rodriguez is serving as acting President under U.S. supervision. Rubio said Venezuela is in a better place and trajectory than five months ago but acknowledged it is not where it ultimately needs to be, stating that true transition requires multiparty, free and fair elections.

Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Coral Gables Republican, raised concerns that the Castro family continues to control Cuba's economy despite indictments and stressed there can be no democratic future for Cuba that leaves the family in power. West Palm Beach Democrat Lois Frankel questioned Rubio about administration pressure on the Gavi Alliance regarding vaccine availability, citing disagreements with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rubio disagreed with the characterization and clarified that the State Department, not HHS, would oversee the Gavi Alliance going forward. Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart, a Hialeah Republican, urged Rubio to consider measures limiting China's influence in the Western Hemisphere.

cards.headline: Florida voters express mixed reactions to November ballot measure on homestead exemption property tax rollback
cards.teaser: Florida voters will decide in November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners. The ballot measure would need 60% approval to pass.
cards.body:
Florida voters will decide this November whether to roll back property taxes by raising the homestead exemption for homeowners, a proposal drawing mixed reactions from West Palm Beach residents. The ballot measure requires 60% approval to pass. A similar proposal to raise the homestead exemption failed in 2018. How much money cities and counties would lose under the plan remains unclear, as does where budget cuts would fall if the measure passes.

Brian Edington supports the idea because it benefits people who permanently live in Florida. He said he is comfortable with local governments spending less and pointed to his neighborhood as an example where cuts could be made, noting that trash services pick up twice a week when once weekly would be adequate. A resident identified only as Stan said he does not want funding eliminated entirely because infrastructure is important, but suggested lowering it to help people. Rosabella Olivares, a shopper in West Palm Beach, expressed concern about reduced funding, saying everything is expensive now. While homeowners were generally supportive of paying less in taxes, renters expressed skepticism. One resident along Clematis Avenue in downtown West Palm Beach said the savings would not reach renters and predicted landlords would raise rent on everybody.

cards.headline: Florida Agriculture Commissioner Ashley Moody files LEO K-9 Protection Act to strengthen penalties for harming police animals
cards.teaser: Ashley Moody filed legislation that strengthens penalties for anyone who intentionally harms animals, including canine officers and patrol horses.
cards.body:
The Plant City Republican filed the LEO K-9 Protection Act, which strengthens penalties for anyone who intentionally harms animals, including canine officers and patrol horses. Moody said these highly trained animals help law enforcement apprehend dangerous criminals, detect narcotics and explosives, assist with searches, find missing persons and save lives. She stated that anyone who intentionally harms police animals in the line of duty should face serious consequences, noting that law enforcement animals serve alongside brave men and women to protect communities.

The legislation is named for K-9 Leo, a Marion County canine deputy who was shot and killed in the line of duty in 2024. In addition to increasing penalties for using deadly weapons against law enforcement animals, the legislation directs the U.S. Department of Transportation to issue regulations permitting emergency medical service providers to transport injured police animals at their discretion. The bill mirrors legislation already introduced in the House by Rep. Aaron Bean, a Fernandina Beach Republican. Moody wants violence against police animals treated the same way assaulting a law enforcement officer is treated, serving as an aggravating factor for criminals already facing other charges.

cards.headline: Hillsborough County Commissioner Joshua Wostal says Tampa CRA may remove Rays ballpark MOU from agenda
cards.teaser: Hillsborough County Commissioner Joshua Wostal indicated that concerns related to Tampa Bay Rays ballpark negotiations could come to a head when the Tampa Community Redevelopment Agency meets next week.
cards.body:
Hillsborough County Commissioner Joshua Wostal said during an appearance on The Ryan Gorman Show that the Tampa Bay Rays memorandum of understanding may face resistance from the Tampa Community Redevelopment Agency next week. Some Tampa City Council members, including swing vote Bill Carlson, have expressed concern about the lack of negotiation by the team with council since the MOU was approved by the city and Hillsborough County last month. Carlson told Florida Politics the Rays primarily negotiated with Tampa Mayor Jane Castor, leaving Council members and many of their requests absent from the negotiation table. However, Carlson noted that Castor is not authorized to negotiate on behalf of the city's CRA. The MOU currently promises $80 million from the city of Tampa and another $100 million from the CRA, in addition to other public dollars.

Wostal said county attorneys confirmed that there is not an executed MOU that has been advertised because the only legal body that can approve or negotiate CRA funds is the Drew Park CRA, not the Tampa Mayor and not the Tampa City Council. The CRA declined to make that vote at their last board meeting and punted it to June, meaning the MOU is not currently executed. Wostal said they will be asking for it to be removed from the agenda, which changes the entire MOU structure because it will now have to go back to all parties for passage again.

cards.headline: Florida Senator Nick DiCeglie endorses Kathleen Peters for Pinellas County Commission District 6 re-election
cards.teaser: Nick DiCeglie endorsed Pinellas County Commissioner Kathleen Peters in her re-election bid for the District 6 seat, describing her as a civil servant with unwavering dedication.
cards.body:
Florida State Senator Nick DiCeglie is endorsing Pinellas County Commissioner Kathleen Peters in her re-election bid for the District 6 seat. DiCeglie described Peters as a civil servant with "unwavering dedication to our communities" and called her the "conservative choice for the Pinellas County Commission." He noted that she has "consistently demonstrated fiscal responsibility while leading on critical local issues like storm resiliency and beach renourishment." Peters, a Republican seeking her second re-election after first securing the seat in 2018, said she was honored to earn DiCeglie's endorsement. She faces a Democratic challenger, David Glenn Jr. DiCeglie's endorsement comes about a week after U.S. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna endorsed Peters and follows a recent endorsement from Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri.

Peters has raised $126,000 through her official campaign account and $24,500 through her affiliated political committee, Florida Speaks, as of the end of March. Glenn has raised $3,400. Peters also benefits from a significant voter registration advantage in District 6, where there are 23,000 more Republicans than Democrats, representing a 25-percentage-point advantage. Peters previously served in the Florida House from 2012 to 2018 and was Mayor of South Pasadena. She currently serves on the boards for Tampa Bay Water, the Tampa Bay Estuary Program, and the Department of Environmental Protection's Tampa Bay Aquatic Preserve Management Plan.

hero.headline: Jupiter Island erosion so severe ocean could breach island at Peck Lake, state warns
hero.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report has documented critical erosion across nearly the entire 11.5-mile coastline of Jupiter Island, raising concerns that a future ocean breakthrough at Peck Lake could split the barrier island in half. The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development already faces risk, to Peck Lake, where a breach would transform a narrow strip of land into an open inlet. This scenario has happened before: a storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s until the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers refilled the area with sand.

According to Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society, a future breach would disrupt ecosystems dependent on a precise balance between fresh and saltwater. The state report identifies numerous sites at risk, including the Joseph Reed Mound, an archaeological site between 3,000 and 4,000 years old that has already lost half its area to erosion. Three wildlife refuges face similar threats: Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry noted that more than 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. A second state assessment warns that erosion is also destroying mangrove swamps essential for habitat and coastal protection, while rising water levels could displace entire species on the island.

The Town of Jupiter Island combats erosion through continuous maintenance efforts. In April 2025, officials completed a major beach renourishment project that deposited enough sand to equal nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said no oceanfront homes face immediate danger only because of ongoing work. He described the situation candidly: "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over. We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it." The town currently spends about $3 million annually in taxpayer dollars on beach renourishment.

The sustainability of this approach remains uncertain. Field warned that a potential breach would require massive state and federal investment to repair. "We would have cataclysmic erosion if we didn't get federal funding and state funding," he said. He emphasized that if beach renourishment funding disappears across Florida, the state's entire coastline could transform rapidly and unfavorably. Field believes the recent FDEP assessment strengthens Jupiter Island's position to secure state and federal funding to address the erosion crisis. The report ultimately underscores how coastal erosion threatens not just homes and infrastructure, but also irreplaceable natural and historical resources.

cards.headline: Summer fertilizer ban begins June 1 in Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties
cards.teaser: Starting June 1 through September 30, residents cannot use fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on lawns or landscaping.
cards.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have implemented a ban on any fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen from June 1 through September 30. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, said the ban is designed to help reduce nutrient-rich runoff during the rainy season, which can cause algae blooms that disrupt waterways like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River.

Harmful algae blooms can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife, and at certain densities, they can release toxins that affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health, according to Skaggs. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a good alternative during the ban for adding nutrients to gardens and landscaping. Ricketts said composting can work like a small trash can and is the easiest and most practical way to add nutrients to a landscape.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue extinguishes nearly 40-acre brush fire in Indiantown
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue put out a large brush fire in Indiantown.
cards.body: Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a brush fire covering nearly 40 acres in Indiantown. The fire was brought under control by fire crews working in the area.

cards.headline: Law enforcement pursuit slows northbound I-95 traffic near Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: A brief law enforcement pursuit caused traffic delays on northbound I-95 near Hobe Sound.
cards.body: A law enforcement pursuit temporarily slowed northbound I-95 traffic near Hobe Sound. The pursuit was brief and impacted traffic flow in the area during the incident.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 30 in St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties
hero.teaser: Residents will not be able to use fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen on lawns or landscaping starting June 30 to reduce algae blooms during rainy season.
hero.body:
Starting June 30, residents in Indian River, Martin, and St. Lucie counties will need to stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The restriction is designed to minimize nutrient-laden runoff during the rainy season, which can trigger harmful algae blooms in local waterways. Jordan Skaggs, with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, explained that these blooms pose a significant threat to the region's aquatic ecosystems, particularly sensitive areas like the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River.

The concern about algae blooms goes beyond simple water discoloration. According to Skaggs, these blooms can shade out plants that fish and wildlife depend on for survival. More troubling still, when algae blooms reach certain concentrations, they can produce toxins harmful to both human and animal health. The cumulative effect threatens the overall health of the entire ecosystem in these waterways.

For residents looking to maintain their gardens and landscaping during the ban, composting offers a practical solution. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends this approach as an alternative to chemical fertilizers. He describes composting as accessible and straightforward, comparing it to using a small trash can to create nutrient-rich material for your landscape.

The composting method allows homeowners to recycle organic waste while simultaneously providing their plants with natural nutrients. This approach supports both environmental protection goals and personal gardening needs. By switching to composting during the fertilizer ban, residents can continue caring for their outdoor spaces while helping prevent the nutrient runoff that leads to problematic algae growth in local waters. The ban represents a community-wide effort to protect the health of the Indian River lagoon, St. Lucie River, and the broader ecosystem these waterways support.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowner watches burglary live on security camera, suspect arrested
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie resident watched a masked man burglarize his apartment in real time on his home security camera Thursday afternoon. Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was arrested and charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling following the incident at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail. The incident began around 3:38 p.m. when the apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home. After checking his live camera feed and spotting the masked intruder, the resident activated his camera's audible siren, causing the suspect to leave briefly. Thibodeau returned and tampered with the camera itself.

Multiple witnesses saw the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. Port St. Lucie Police arrived to find clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Thibodeau exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from multiple sources throughout the complex, including doorbell cameras that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. Police found evidence that Thibodeau had attempted to obstruct security cameras and that a watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen during the burglary.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island faces critical erosion threatening to split island at Peck Lake
cards.teaser: A state report warns that erosion along Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile coastline has become so severe the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half.
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report warns that nearly the entire 11.5-mile coastline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, threatening roads, buildings, drainage systems, natural habitats, wildlife and ancient sites. The erosion has become so severe that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. A storm previously breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. Among the sites at risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site already half lost to erosion, along with wildlife refuges including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. There are over 33 threatened and endangered species in these areas.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues fighting erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field noted that about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment annually. He warned that if funding for beach renourishment in Florida ever disappears, "the coastline of Florida is going to change very quickly."

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban starts June 1 in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
hero.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties must stop using fertilizers that contain phosphorus or nitrogen. The restriction remains in effect through September 30, covering the region's rainy season when nutrient runoff poses the greatest environmental risk.

The ban targets a significant environmental problem. According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the goal is to reduce nutrient-rich runoff that flows into local waterways during heavy rains. This runoff can trigger harmful algae blooms in sensitive ecosystems like the Indian River Lagoon and St. Lucie River. Skaggs explained that these blooms create multiple problems for aquatic environments. "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," Skaggs said. The impacts can be severe depending on bloom density. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health."

Residents should prepare alternatives now to maintain their landscaping during the ban period. Grantly Ricketts, director of University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as a practical solution. This method provides essential nutrients to gardens and landscaping without violating the restriction on commercial fertilizers. "It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape." Composting allows homeowners to recycle organic materials while supporting healthy plant growth.

The four-month ban reflects growing awareness of how fertilizer runoff damages Florida's waterways. By restricting nutrient applications during the season when heavy rainfall washes chemicals into rivers and lagoons, the three counties aim to protect both environmental and public health. Residents who plan ahead by starting compost systems or exploring other organic alternatives can maintain their landscaping without contributing to the algae bloom problem.
